body.text: Why sanding is not optional before a quality stain job

Stain performs best when it can penetrate into open wood grain rather than sit on a rough or partially finished surface. A deck that has weathered for a few seasons, or one that still has old, flaking stain clinging to it, will absorb a new coat unevenly no matter how good the product is. Restore My Deck sands every restoration and most staining projects with an 80-grit buff sander before applying any finish, because skipping this step is one of the most common reasons a fresh stain job looks patchy or fails early.
What buff sanding actually does to the wood

An 80-grit buff sander removes splinters, smooths rough or weathered spots, and lifts loose or flaking remnants of old finish from the surface. It also opens the top layer of wood grain slightly, which increases the surface area available for stain or sealant to soak into. This matters most on decks that have gone a few years between refinishing, since UV exposure and freeze-thaw cycling roughen the wood's surface over time even if it has not visibly failed yet. Sanding resets that surface so the new finish has a clean, consistent base to bond to.
Pressure-treated pine versus cedar under the sander

Pressure-treated pine and cedar respond differently to sanding. Pine is softer and can fuzz or gouge more easily under aggressive grit or excessive pressure, so we favour a lighter, more controlled pass tuned to the wood's density. Cedar is denser and holds up to a slightly firmer sanding pass, which helps bring out its natural grain pattern more distinctly. Since so many decks across Kitchener, Waterloo and Cambridge use pressure-treated pine, we default to a careful approach and adjust upward only when the wood and its condition call for it.

body.text: Sanding is best done on a dry deck in stable weather, since damp wood does not sand evenly and can clog sandpaper quickly. In our region, that generally means late spring through early fall, avoiding the humid stretches right after a rain. We schedule sanding immediately before staining or sealing whenever possible, since freshly sanded wood is more exposed to moisture and dirt until it is coated, and leaving too much time between the two steps can undo some of the benefit.
Sanding is most effective when scheduled right before staining or sealing, so freshly opened grain does not sit exposed to moisture or dirt.
How sanding fits into a full restoration

Sanding rarely stands entirely on its own. It usually follows a cleaning step, since sanding over dirt or grime just grinds debris into the wood rather than removing it, and it usually precedes staining or sealing, since sanded wood left bare will absorb moisture and dirt quickly. Our /deck-restoration service bundles cleaning, repair, sanding and staining into one project for decks that need the full treatment, while a standalone sanding service suits decks that are structurally fine and clean but need a smoother surface before a fresh coat of stain or sealer.
What sanding will and won't remove

Sanding effectively removes most of an old finish and smooths the surface underneath, but how much comes off depends on how many previous coats of stain or paint have built up over the years. Decks with a single light stain application sand down cleanly, while decks with multiple layers of solid stain or paint may need a heavier pass or a combination of sanding and stripping to get back to bare, even wood. faqs.q: How often should my deck be sanded?
faqs.a: It depends on wood type, sun exposure and usage, but most decks benefit from sanding every 2 to 3 years, typically as part of a re-staining or restoration project.

faqs.q: Can all types of decks be sanded?
faqs.a: Most wood decks can be sanded, though pressure-treated pine and cedar require different approaches since pine is softer and more prone to fuzzing under aggressive sanding.

faqs.q: Will sanding remove all of the old stain or paint?
faqs.a: Sanding removes most of an existing finish, but complete removal depends on how many coats have built up. Heavily coated decks may need extra passes or additional stripping.

faqs.q: Is there a risk of damaging the wood while sanding?
faqs.a: We use professional-grade equipment and adjust technique to wood type and condition, which keeps the risk of surface damage low while still achieving an even, ready-to-finish surface.

faqs.q: Should I book sanding separately from staining?
faqs.a: Sanding is most effective when scheduled right before staining or sealing, since freshly sanded, open wood grain is more vulnerable to moisture and dirt if it sits uncoated too long.
